sections.body: Agent workflows in finance are the places where a language model or a small team of them is wired into a real desk process rather than a demo. The work is document heavy and deadline heavy: a request for proposal lands and someone has to assemble a response, a trade is negotiated over the counter and terms have to be captured, an investment committee needs a memo by morning, a comparable company set drifts out of date, a settlement instruction has to match. What the agents actually do now is read the incoming material, pull the relevant figures from internal systems, draft the first pass, and route it to a human for sign off. The value is measured in hours returned and in fewer transcription errors, not in autonomous decision making. Every one of these steps still ends with a named person who is accountable for what goes out.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The drafting and summarising parts are the most mature, because the failure mode is a bad paragraph that a reviewer catches. Negotiation is the least mature, since an agent that commits to terms creates obligations, and the honest position is that most firms keep a human in the loop for anything binding. Settlement automation is old technology in many shops, and the new work is mostly about translating messy messages into the formats the existing pipes already expect. The limits are consistent across all five areas: the agent does not know what it does not know, it cannot verify a counterparty, and it will produce a confident sentence from a stale source unless the retrieval layer is disciplined. Audit trails, permissions and versioning are the unglamorous parts that decide whether any of this survives a compliance review. Nothing here removes the need for the reviewer, and nothing here is a substitute for the firm's own obligations.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages follow one deal from pitch to cash. Drafting Proposal Responses is the entry point, where the agent assembles a bid from prior submissions and firm data, and it is the page to read first if you want to see the pattern at its simplest. Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets sits in the middle of the trade, and it is the page that raises the hard questions about authority and limits. Investment Committee Memos is the internal counterpart, where the agent turns a model and a thesis into a document a committee can argue with. Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current is the maintenance page, the unglamorous recurring job that keeps every other document honest, and Automating Trade Settlement is the back end, where the trade becomes a payment and the tolerance for error is lowest. Read together they show the same architecture applied at five points, and a reader can enter at whichever point matches the process they already own.
